title: General Liability Insurance for Small Business: Coverage, Cost and How to Buy
seoTitle: General Liability Insurance: Simple 2026 Guide
excerpt: What general liability insurance covers for a small business, what it leaves out, what it costs in 2026 and how to buy the right policy with confidence.
content:
General liability insurance pays for claims that your business caused injury to someone else or damaged their property, plus your legal defense. Clients and landlords ask for it more than any other cover. The U.S. Small Business Administration says any business may need it. This guide shows what the policy covers, what it leaves out, what it costs and how to buy one.

Key takeaways

  • General liability covers third-party bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury, plus legal defense costs.
  • It does not cover your own employees, your own property, professional mistakes or vehicles; those need other policies.
  • Small businesses with Insureon paid a median of about $45 a month in 2026, but your price depends on your industry, location and limits.

This article is general information, not insurance or legal advice. Coverage depends on the exact policy wording and your state. Speak to a licensed insurance agent or broker before you buy or change a policy.

What general liability insurance covers

A standard commercial general liability (CGL) policy usually covers four things:

  • Bodily injury to other people, such as a customer who slips in your shop.
  • Property damage you cause to someone else's property, such as a contractor who damages a client's floor.
  • Personal and advertising injury, such as claims of libel, slander or copying someone's advertising.
  • Legal defense costs for a covered claim, even one that turns out to be false.

The ad part matters for any business that markets itself. Say someone claims your ad used their slogan, photo or brand name. That claim may fall under this cover, based on your policy. It is still far better to use only content you own or have paid to use.

What general liability does not cover

Policies also leave out harm you cause on purpose and fines in your contracts. Many limit cover for some trades. Read the list of what is not covered, or ask your agent to walk you through it.

Who needs general liability cover?

The SBA's business insurance guide lists general liability as coverage any business may need. You are especially likely to need it if:

  • Customers or suppliers visit your premises.
  • You work at clients' homes or sites, as contractors, cleaners and installers do.
  • A landlord, client or contract asks for a certificate of insurance.
  • You advertise, run a website or post on social media.

Businesses with employees also need workers' compensation in most states, and the rules are set by each state. General liability does not replace it.

How much does general liability insurance cost?

Insureon reported in March 2026 that its small business customers paid a median of about $45 a month for general liability. In the same data:

  • 22% paid less than $30 a month, and 41% paid between $30 and $60.
  • Annual premiums ranged from about $265 to $3,030.
  • 85% chose limits of $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate.

These figures come from one firm's customers, and many of them are low-risk. Treat them as a guide, not a quote. A roofer will pay far more than a consultant who works from home.

What affects your premium

  • Your industry and the work you do.
  • Policy limits and deductible.
  • Your location and state.
  • Number of employees, payroll and annual revenue.
  • The size and condition of your premises.
  • Years in business and your claims history.

Business owner's policy (BOP) vs general liability

A business owner's policy (BOP) bundles general liability with cover for your own building and kit. It often costs less than buying both on their own. The SBA describes it as a package that suits most small business owners. If you own equipment, stock or furniture, ask for a BOP quote alongside a standalone general liability quote.

Occurrence vs claims-made policies

Most policies are written on an occurrence basis. They cover events that happen while the policy is live, even if the claim comes years later. A claims-made policy covers claims made while the policy is live. If you are offered claims-made cover, ask about the start date it looks back to and "tail" cover for when it ends.

How to buy general liability insurance: seven steps

  1. List your risks. Who visits you, where you work and what could go wrong.
  2. Check what clients and landlords require. Note the limits and any "additional insured" wording in your contracts.
  3. Choose limits. $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate is common, but some contracts require more.
  4. Talk to a licensed agent or broker. Independent agents can compare several insurers for you.
  5. Compare at least three quotes. Compare limits, deductibles, exclusions and the insurer's financial strength, not just price.
  6. Ask about a BOP if you also need property cover.
  7. Get your certificate of insurance and review the policy every year, or when your work changes.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Buying the cheapest policy without reading the exclusions.
  • Assuming general liability covers your employees or professional errors.
  • Choosing limits below what your contracts require.
  • Forgetting to update the policy when you add services, staff or locations.
  • Using photos or content in your marketing that you do not have rights to.

Frequently asked questions

Is general liability insurance required by law?

Usually not by law, but clients, landlords and many contracts require it, and some licenses and permits ask for proof of coverage. Workers' compensation, not general liability, is the policy most states require for businesses with employees.

How much general liability cover do I need?

Many small businesses choose $1 million per occurrence and $2 million aggregate, which Insureon says 85% of its customers selected. Check your contracts and leases, because some require higher limits.

Does general liability cover my own injuries?

No. It covers injuries to third parties. Your own injuries are usually covered by health insurance, and your employees' work injuries by workers' compensation.

What is a certificate of insurance?

A certificate of insurance is a one-page document from your insurer or agent that proves you have coverage and shows your limits. Clients and landlords often ask for one before you start work.

Does SEMRS sell insurance?

No. SEMRS is a digital marketing agency and does not sell or arrange insurance. If you are an insurance agency that wants more leads, read our guide to insurance agency marketing or see our pricing.

Running a small business? Read more in the Business Insurance category or our guide to small business loans for marketing.

title: Personal Injury Lawyer Advertising That Works: Channels, Costs and Bar Rules

excerpt: Personal injury lawyer advertising explained: the channels that bring cases, what clicks and leads cost, and the bar rules every ad must follow.
content:
Personal injury lawyer advertising works when it reaches people in the hours and days after an accident, when they search, call and compare firms. The firms that do well pick a few channels, answer the phone fast and track which ads sign cases. This guide covers the main channels, what they cost, how to measure them and the ethics rules your ads must follow.

Key takeaways

  • Injury clients usually search on Google and call within days, so search ads, Local Services Ads and your Business Profile come first.
  • Legal clicks and leads are among the most expensive in Google Ads, so track cost per signed case, not cost per click.
  • Every ad must follow your state bar's advertising rules: no false or misleading claims and no promised results.

This article is general information about marketing, not legal advice. Lawyer advertising rules differ by state, so check your state bar's rules or ask an ethics counsel before you run an ad.

How injury clients choose a lawyer

Most people have never hired a lawyer before their accident. They search on a phone, often from home or a hospital, with words like "car accident lawyer near me". They look at reviews, call two or three firms and hire the one that answers, sounds calm and explains the next step.

That means your advertising has three jobs:

  1. Be visible where people search in the first days.
  2. Earn trust quickly with reviews, clear practice pages and real photos of your team.
  3. Convert the call with fast answers, a friendly intake script and a clear free consultation offer.

The main personal injury lawyer advertising channels

Google Search ads

Search ads show your firm when someone types a specific phrase, such as "truck accident attorney Houston". You choose the keywords, the area and the hours. They are fast to start and easy to measure, but they are costly in legal. In the 2025 Google Ads benchmarks, attorneys and legal services had the highest average cost per click at $8.58, against $5.26 across all industries. The average legal cost per lead was $131.63.

Keep campaigns tight: one case type per ad group, a matching landing page and a long list of negative keywords such as "jobs", "salary" and "free legal aid". Our guide to Google Ads cost shows how to set a budget from the value of a case.

Local Services Ads

Local Services Ads show above normal search ads with a "Google Screened" badge. You pay per lead (a call or message), not per click. Google lists personal injury lawyer services as an eligible category, and your firm must pass Google's screening first. Compare both formats in Local Services Ads vs Google Ads.

Google Business Profile and reviews

Your Business Profile decides whether you appear in the map results. Fill in every field, pick "Personal injury attorney" as the main category, add office photos and ask every satisfied client for a review. Our Google Business Profile guide walks through each step.

SEO and helpful content

Search engine optimization brings calls you do not pay for per click. It takes months, but it keeps working. Build one page for each case type and city you serve, and answer real questions: "How long does a car accident claim take?" or "Who pays my medical bills?" Our guide to law firm SEO covers the full plan.

TV, radio, billboards and social media

Mass media builds name recognition in a market, so callers already know your firm when they search. It costs much more and is harder to track. Use a unique phone number and web address for each campaign so you can see what it brings in. On social media, short videos that explain common questions work better than "call now" posts.

A simple advertising plan for a small injury firm

Start with the channels closest to the moment of need. Add brand advertising only when intake and tracking are working, or you pay to make the phone ring with no way to know what it earned.

What personal injury lawyer advertising costs

Costs depend on your market, case types and competition. A few rules of thumb help:

  • Budget from a signed case, not a click. If one case in ten leads signs, and you can afford $1,500 to sign a case, you can pay up to $150 a lead.
  • Count every cost. Include agency fees, intake staff and call tracking, not only ad spend.
  • Compare channels by cost per signed case. A cheap lead that never signs is not cheap.
  • Expect a learning month. The first weeks of any paid campaign are mostly testing.

Bar rules every injury lawyer ad must follow

Personal injury lawyer advertising is regulated by each state's rules of professional conduct. Most states base their rules on the ABA Model Rules. Model Rule 7.1 bans false or misleading communication about a lawyer's services. Common problems include:

  • Promising results or implying past verdicts mean a new client will win.
  • Using actors or dramatizations without the disclaimers your state requires.
  • Calling yourself a "specialist" without a certification your state recognizes.
  • Paying for referrals outside the limited exceptions in your state's rules.
  • Soliciting accident victims directly by phone or in person, which most states restrict.

Some state bars also want ads filed or kept on record. Keep a copy of every ad, landing page and script with the date it ran.

How to measure your advertising

  1. Use call tracking with a separate number per channel.
  2. Record the source of every new case in your intake software.
  3. Tag links in ads, emails and social posts. Our free UTM builder creates them in seconds.
  4. Review each month: leads, signed cases and cost per signed case by channel.
  5. Move budget toward the channels that sign cases at the lowest cost.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best advertising for personal injury lawyers?

For most firms, Google search ads, Local Services Ads and a strong Business Profile bring the fastest calls, because people search right after an accident. SEO builds lower-cost cases over time. TV and billboards work best for firms that already have intake and tracking in place.

How much do personal injury lawyers spend on advertising?

It varies widely by market. Legal had the highest average Google Ads cost per click in the 2025 benchmarks at $8.58, with an average cost per lead of $131.63. Set your budget from the value of a signed case and the share of leads that sign.

Can lawyers advertise on Facebook and Instagram?

Yes, if the ads follow your state's lawyer advertising rules. Avoid testimonials or results claims your state restricts, and keep a copy of every ad.

Is it legal for a law firm to pay for leads?

Paying for advertising, including pay-per-lead ads such as Local Services Ads, is generally allowed. Paying someone to recommend you is restricted in most states. Check your state's version of Model Rule 7.2.

Can SEMRS run our law firm advertising?

Yes. SEMRS sets up and manages Google Ads and Local Services Ads in accounts your firm owns, with call tracking and a monthly report on cost per lead. See our paid ads services and pricing.

title: Google Ads for Small Business: A Beginner Guide to Your First Campaign
seoTitle: Google Ads for Small Business: Simple 2026 Guide
excerpt: Google Ads for small business in plain steps: how billing works, how to set a budget, build your first search campaign and avoid costly beginner mistakes.
content:
Google Ads for small business can bring calls and enquiries within days, because your ad shows when someone searches for exactly what you sell. You set the budget, pay only when someone clicks and can stop at any time. This beginner guide explains how billing works, how to plan a budget and how to build your first search campaign without wasting money.

Key takeaways

  • Start with one search campaign, a small list of high-intent keywords and one matching landing page.
  • Set conversion tracking before you spend, so you judge ads by leads, not clicks.
  • Your daily budget is an average: Google can spend up to twice it on a busy day but bills no more than 30.4 times it in a month.

How Google Ads works

Google Ads is an auction. When someone searches, Google picks which ads to show and in what order. It looks at your bid, the quality of your ad and landing page, and how relevant they are to the search. You usually pay per click, so an ad that shows but gets no clicks costs nothing.

There are several campaign types. For a small business, start with Search. Search ads answer a need someone is typing right now, such as "emergency plumber Denver" or "tax accountant near me". Display, video and Performance Max campaigns can work later, once you know which searches bring customers.

What Google Ads costs a small business

You choose the budget, so there is no minimum spend. What you pay per click depends on your industry and area. In the 2025 benchmarks, the average cost per click across industries was $5.26 and the average cost per lead was $70.11. Legal, home services and dental clicks cost more than average.

How billing works matters for planning. Google's help page explains that a campaign can spend up to twice its average daily budget on some days. Over a month, it will charge no more than 30.4 times the daily budget. So a $20 daily budget means about $608 a month at most.

Our guide to Google Ads cost shows how to work out a budget from what a customer is worth.

Google Ads for small business: your first campaign

  1. Set up conversion tracking. Track calls, form submissions and bookings. Without it, you cannot tell good keywords from bad ones.
  2. Choose a Search campaign and turn off the Display Network and search partners at first.
  3. Set your location to the area you actually serve, using "presence" (people in the area), not just interest.
  4. Pick 10 to 20 keywords that show buying intent, such as "boiler repair Leeds" or "same day dentist Austin".
  5. Add negative keywords such as "jobs", "free", "DIY" and "course" so you do not pay for the wrong searches.
  6. Write three ads per ad group with the service, the area and a clear next step.
  7. Send clicks to a matching page. A plumber's "boiler repair" ad should land on a boiler repair page with a phone number at the top.
  8. Set a daily budget you can sustain for at least a month, so Google has time to learn.

Keywords and match types

Start with exact and phrase match. Broad match can work with smart bidding and good conversion data, but it spends faster on loosely related searches. Check the search terms report every week and add any irrelevant terms as negatives.

Local ads and free Google tools

Not all Google advertising is paid. A complete Google Business Profile puts you in map results for free, and it often brings more calls than ads for local services. Many service businesses also qualify for Local Services Ads, which charge per lead and carry a Google badge. Our comparison of Local Services Ads vs Google Ads explains when each one fits.

Common beginner mistakes to avoid

  • No conversion tracking. You end up optimizing for clicks that never call.
  • Too many keywords at once. The budget spreads thin and nothing gets enough data.
  • Sending everyone to the home page. Each ad needs a page about that exact service.
  • Accepting every recommendation. Some suggestions raise spend without raising leads. Read each one first.
  • Changing everything daily. Campaigns need one to two weeks of data before big changes.
  • Ignoring the phone. If calls go to voicemail, the best ads in the world will not help.

How to measure results

The best business credit cards for advertising spend pay you back on the ads you already buy, such as Google, Meta and other online ads, without high fees or interest eating the reward.   • If you need time to pay, a 0% intro APR card costs less than any reward is worth.
  • Business cards lack some consumer protections, and most require a personal guarantee.

This article is general information, not financial advice. Card terms change often, so check the issuer's current terms before you apply. SEMRS has no affiliate or paid relationship with any card issuer named here.

Why put advertising on a business card

Ad platforms such as Google Ads and Meta charge a card again and again as you spend. A business card keeps those costs apart from personal spending, gives you one monthly statement and can earn rewards on money you would spend anyway. It also gives you a short grace period: when you pay the full balance by the due date, you usually pay no interest.

The risk is carrying a balance. Card interest rates are high, so interest on unpaid ad spend can cost more than the ads earn.

The three types of business credit cards

Protections business cards do not have

title: Dental Marketing: How Dentists Get New Patients

content:
Dental marketing is how a practice gets found, trusted and booked by new patients, and how it keeps the patients it already has. Most new patients start with a search such as "dentist near me" and choose from the map results, reviews and the practice website. This guide sets out eight ways to win patients, what each costs in time and money, and the privacy and review rules every practice must follow.

Key takeaways

  • Your Google Business Profile, reviews and website decide most first bookings, so fix them before you buy ads.
  • Use paid search for high-value treatments such as implants, Invisalign and emergency care, with one page per treatment.
  • Patient privacy rules and the FTC review rule apply to all dental marketing, including social media.

This article is general information, not legal advice. Patient privacy and advertising rules vary by country and state, so check your dental board's rules and HIPAA guidance before you use patient information in marketing.

How patients choose a dentist

Patients look for three things: a practice close to home or work, good reviews and an easy way to book. Many also check whether you take their insurance, offer evening or weekend hours and treat nervous patients. If your profile and website answer those questions quickly, you win the booking.

8 ways to get new dental patients

1. Complete your Google Business Profile

Choose "Dentist" as the main category and add services such as "Cosmetic dentist" or "Emergency dental service" where they fit. Add hours, insurance plans, accessibility details and real photos of your team and rooms. Our Google Business Profile guide covers every field.

2. Ask every happy patient for a review

Reviews are one of the strongest local signals. Ask in person at checkout, then send a short text or email with a direct link. Our free Google review link generator makes that link in seconds. Reply to every review in a calm, general way, and never confirm that the reviewer is a patient.

3. Build a fast website with one page per treatment

Patients search for treatments, not for "services". Give implants, Invisalign, whitening, children's dentistry and emergency care their own pages. Each page should explain the treatment, what to expect, prices or payment options, and how to book. Keep the site fast on phones and accessible to everyone; our ADA website compliance guide explains what that means.

4. Use local SEO and helpful content

Answer real questions in short articles: "How long does an implant take to heal?" or "What counts as a dental emergency?" Add your city to page titles where it reads naturally. Our guide to SEO for small business explains the basics of dental SEO marketing step by step.

5. Run Google Ads for high-value treatments

Paid search works well for treatments with high value or urgent need. Keep it tight: one campaign per treatment, keywords with the city name, and ads that send people to the matching page. Dental clicks are among the more expensive in local advertising, so track booked appointments, not clicks. Our guide to Google Ads cost explains how to set a budget.

6. Make booking easy

Put the phone number at the top of every page and add online booking if your system allows it. Answer calls quickly, and call back missed calls the same day. Many new patients book with the first practice that answers.

7. Keep patients with email and text reminders

Recall reminders, hygiene appointments and simple newsletters keep chairs full. Get clear consent before you send marketing messages, and keep appointment reminders separate from promotions.

8. Show your team on social media

Short posts about your team, your community and simple care tips build trust. Never post patient photos, X-rays or stories without written authorization.

Dental marketing budget and timeline

Start with the free and low-cost steps, then add ads once your pages and booking process are ready.

Privacy and review rules for dental marketing

Patient privacy. In the US, the HIPAA Privacy Rule generally requires a patient's written authorization before you use their health information for marketing. That includes testimonials, before-and-after photos and stories that identify a patient. The HHS marketing guidance explains the rule.

Reviews. The FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect on October 21, 2024. It bans fake reviews, buying positive reviews and hiding negative ones. You may ask for honest reviews; you may not reward only good ones. Staff reviews must disclose that the writer works for you.

Claims. Avoid "best dentist in town" or guaranteed results unless you can prove them. Some dental boards also limit how you describe specialties.

How to measure what works

  1. Ask every new patient how they found you and record it.
  2. Use call tracking for ads and your Business Profile.
  3. Track bookings from your website forms.
  4. Review monthly: new patients by source, cost per new patient and recall rates.

For most practices, a complete Google Business Profile, steady reviews and a fast website with treatment pages bring the most new patients for the least money. Google Ads adds patients for high-value treatments once those basics are in place.

It depends on your goals and market. Start by working out what a new patient is worth over a year, then decide how much you can pay to win one. Track cost per new patient by channel and move budget to what works.

Can dentists use patient testimonials in marketing?

Yes, with care. In the US you generally need the patient's written authorization to use their health information in marketing, and testimonials must be real and not paid for being positive.

Should a dental practice hire a marketing agency?

An agency makes sense when you lack the time or skills in-house. Ask for clear reporting on new patients, ownership of your ad accounts and website, and a written scope with no long lock-in.

title: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) Explained for Small Businesses
seoTitle: Generative Engine Optimization: Simple 2026 Guide
excerpt: Generative engine optimization (GEO) explained: how AI answers pick sources, what Google says about AI Overviews and steps that make pages easy to cite.
content:
Generative engine optimization, or GEO, means making your content easy for AI answer engines to find, understand and cite. Tools such as Google's AI Overviews, ChatGPT search and Perplexity write an answer and link a handful of sources. GEO is about being one of those sources. This guide explains how it works, what Google itself says and the practical steps that help a small business get cited.

Key takeaways

  • GEO builds on SEO: AI answers mostly draw on pages that are already crawlable, indexed and trusted.
  • Clear answers, facts with sources and well-structured pages are easier for AI tools to quote.
  • Google says there are no extra requirements or special files needed to appear in AI Overviews.

What generative engine optimization means

Traditional search shows a list of links. Generative engines write an answer first and cite sources inside or beside it. The term "generative engine optimization" comes from a 2023 research paper by Aggarwal and colleagues, later accepted at the KDD 2024 conference. In their tests, methods such as adding citations, quotations and statistics improved a source's visibility in AI answers by up to 40%, with results varying by topic.

For a business, the goal is simple: when someone asks an AI tool a question in your field, your page should be the clearest, most trustworthy answer it can find.

GEO vs SEO

They overlap far more than they differ. A page that is slow, blocked from crawling or thin will not do well in either.

What Google says about AI Overviews

Google's guidance on AI features and your website is clear on several points:

  • There are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. A page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet.
  • You do not need new machine-readable files, special "AI text files" or new markup for Google.
  • Normal SEO basics apply: allow crawling, use internal links, offer a good page experience and keep structured data consistent with the visible text.
  • Clicks from AI features are counted in Search Console's Performance report under the "Web" search type.

So, for Google, generative engine optimization is mostly good SEO done well. Other AI tools have their own crawlers, so check that your site does not block the ones you want.

How to optimize for AI answers

  1. Answer the question first. Put a direct, two or three sentence answer at the top of the page or section.
  2. Use clear headings that match how people ask: "How much does a roof repair cost in Denver?"
  3. Back claims with sources. Cite official data and original research, and add the date you checked it.
  4. Add specific facts. Prices, steps, timelines and examples are easier to quote than general claims.
  5. Use structured data that matches the page, such as Organization, LocalBusiness, Article and FAQ. Our free schema markup generator helps.
  6. Show who is behind the content. Author names, credentials, an about page and real contact details build trust.
  7. Keep pages fresh. Update prices, rules and screenshots at least once a year.
  8. Earn mentions elsewhere. Reviews, local press and industry directories help AI tools trust your brand.

Do you need an llms.txt file?

An llms.txt file is a short summary of your site's most useful pages, written for AI tools. Google says it does not need one, and support among other AI tools is uneven. It is cheap to add and harmless, so some sites publish one as a simple map. Our free llms.txt generator builds one in minutes. Do not expect it to replace good pages.

Generative AI in marketing: use it carefully

Generative AI can help draft outlines, summaries and first versions of pages. But AI tools favor accurate, specific, trustworthy sources. Content written by AI and published without checks tends to be generic, and it can contain errors. Use AI for speed and people for facts and judgment. Our guide to AI marketing tools shows a safe workflow with human approval.

How to measure GEO

  • Search Console: watch impressions and clicks for question-style queries.
  • Referral traffic: check analytics for visits from AI tools such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Copilot and Gemini.
  • Manual checks: ask AI tools your main customer questions each month and note who gets cited.
  • Brand searches: a rise in people searching your name can follow AI mentions.

Frequently asked questions

What is generative engine optimization?

Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the practice of making your content easy for AI answer engines to find, understand and cite. It builds on SEO with a focus on clear answers, evidence and trust.

Is GEO different from SEO?

It overlaps heavily. Google says pages need no special work beyond being indexed and eligible for snippets. The difference is focus: GEO pays extra attention to quotable answers, sources and brand trust.

How do I get my business into Google's AI Overviews?

Make sure your pages can be crawled and indexed, answer common questions clearly, keep structured data accurate and build trust with reviews and real business details. Google does not offer a way to request inclusion.

Does AI search reduce website traffic?

It can reduce clicks for simple questions that the answer fully covers. Google says clicks from AI Overviews tend to be higher quality. Pages with depth, tools, prices and local details still earn visits.

Yes. Every SEMRS SEO plan includes GEO work: answer-first structure, schema and content AI tools can quote. See our SEO services and pricing.

Website builders for small business let you launch a professional site without writing code. The main choices are WordPress, Wix, Squarespace and Shopify, and each suits a different kind of business. The four main options

WordPress is free, open-source software that you install on your own hosting. It runs about 38% of all websites, according to W3Techs, and offers thousands of themes and plugins. You own the files and can move hosts at any time.

Wix is a hosted, drag-and-drop builder. Hosting, security and updates are included in the plan. It is easy for beginners and has apps for bookings, stores and events.

How to choose a website builder

  2. Count the pages and features you need in the next two years, not just today.

A Google Ads agency plans, builds and manages your paid search campaigns so you get more leads or sales for your budget. A good one sets up tracking, cuts wasted spend and reports results in plain words. A poor one can lock you into contracts, hide data and judge success by clicks. This guide explains what agencies do, how they charge and the nine questions to ask before you sign.

Key takeaways

  • Insist that the ad account is in your name, with your card paying Google directly.
  • Ask how the agency tracks leads and sales; reports should show cost per lead, not just clicks.
  • Compare fees in dollars at your real budget, and avoid long lock-in contracts.

What a Google Ads agency does

  • Sets up tracking for calls, forms, bookings and sales before spending.
  • Researches keywords and builds campaigns around services and areas.
  • Writes ads and recommends landing page changes.
  • Manages bids and budgets, adding negative keywords to cut waste.
  • Tests ads, offers and pages over time.
  • Reports results and next steps each month.

When to hire an agency, and when not to

An agency makes sense when ads are a main source of customers, your budget is large enough that waste hurts, or you do not have the time to check campaigns every week. If you spend a small amount and have time to learn, managing your own account can work. Our Google Ads for small business guide explains the basics.

How Google Ads agencies charge

Some agencies also charge a setup fee. Always ask for the fee in dollars at your real budget. For example, SEMRS charges 15% of each platform's ad spend, with a minimum of $30 a month per platform, and your card pays Google directly. Our guide to Google Ads cost helps you plan the ad budget itself.

What Google Partner status means

The Google Partners badge shows that an agency meets Google's current requirements. According to Google's help page, these include an optimization score of at least 70% on its manager account, at least $10,000 in ad spend across managed accounts over 90 days and certified staff. It is a useful sign of activity and training, but it does not prove results for a business like yours. Ask for the agency's approach and references too.

9 questions to ask a Google Ads agency

  1. Who owns the ad account? It should be in your name, with admin access for you.
  2. How will you track leads and sales? Expect call, form and booking tracking before launch.
  3. What do you charge, in dollars, at my budget? Get setup and monthly fees in writing.
  4. How long is the contract? Monthly terms with notice are fairer than a one-year lock-in.
  5. Who will manage my account? Ask about their experience and how many accounts they run.
  6. What will you do in the first 90 days? A clear plan beats vague promises.

  8. How do you handle Google's recommendations? Good agencies review each one, not accept all.
  9. Can you share examples from similar businesses? Ask for real, checkable examples.

Red flags to avoid

  • Guaranteed rankings or results. No one controls Google's auction.
  • The agency owns your account. If you leave, you may lose your data and history.
  • Hidden ad spend. You should see exactly what Google charged.
  • Reports full of clicks and impressions but no leads or sales.
  • Long contracts with exit fees before the agency has proven itself.

How to measure your agency

Partner status shows the agency meets Google's spend, performance and certification requirements. It is a good sign, but it does not guarantee results for your business. Judge the agency's plan, reporting and references as well.

Yes. The account should be in your business's name, with your payment method, so you keep your data and history if you change agencies.

title: Marketing Automation Software for Small Business: Features, Costs and How to Start
seoTitle: Marketing Automation Software: 2026 Simple Guide
excerpt: Marketing automation software for small business: what it automates, features that matter, how pricing works and five automations worth setting up first.
content:
Marketing automation software sends the right message at the right time without you doing it by hand. It can welcome new subscribers, follow up on enquiries, remind customers to book again and pass hot leads to sales. For a small business, the goal is not more email. It is fewer missed follow-ups. This guide covers what these tools do, which features matter, how pricing works and the first automations to set up.

Key takeaways

  • Start with a few simple automations: a welcome series, enquiry follow-up and review requests.
  • Choose software that connects to your CRM, website forms and store, so contact data stays in one place.
  • Collect clear consent, and follow email and text message rules in every automation.

What marketing automation software does

Marketing automation software runs actions when a trigger happens. A trigger can be a form submission, a purchase, a date or a click. The action can be an email, a text, a tag, a task for your team or a change in the contact's stage.

Common uses for small businesses:

  • Welcome series for new subscribers.
  • Lead follow-up after a quote request or booking.
  • Abandoned cart emails for online stores.
  • Review requests after a job is finished.
  • Re-booking reminders for services people repeat, such as cleaning or dental checkups.
  • Lead scoring that flags people who visit pricing pages or open several emails.

Features that matter for a small business

How pricing works

Most tools charge by the number of contacts, the number of emails sent or the number of users. Many have free plans with basic email automation; full multi-step workflows often need a higher plan. HubSpot is one example: in November 2026, its Marketing Hub had a free plan with simple email automation, a Starter plan from $20 per seat a month and a Professional plan with full workflows from $800 a month plus a one-time $3,000 onboarding fee.

The lesson: price the plan that includes the automation you actually need, at the list size you expect next year. Our guide to email marketing platforms compares free plans for email-first tools.

Five automations to set up first

  1. Welcome series. Three to five emails over two weeks: thank you, who you are, your most useful guide, a customer story and a clear offer.
  2. Enquiry follow-up. An instant reply when someone requests a quote, then a reminder to your team if no one has called within an hour.
  3. Review request. A short email or text a day after the job, with a direct review link. Our free Google review link generator makes the link.
  4. Re-booking reminder. A reminder when a service is due again.
  5. Win-back email. A friendly check-in for customers who have not bought in a while.

How to choose marketing automation software

  1. List your top three flows and check each tool can build them on the plan you will buy.
  2. Check integrations with your CRM, website forms, booking system and store. Our guide to the best CRM for small business explains why one contact record matters.
  3. Test the workflow builder with a free plan or trial.
  4. Check deliverability tools such as domain authentication.
  5. Compare the price at double your current list size.
  6. Check data export, so you can leave with your contacts and consent records.

Email and text message rules

Automation sends more messages, so compliance matters more. In the US, commercial email must follow the FTC's CAN-SPAM rules: honest headers and subject lines, your postal address and a working unsubscribe that is honored within 10 business days. Marketing texts are stricter. Under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, you generally need the person's prior express written consent before sending automated marketing texts. Other countries, such as Canada and the UK, require consent before you email.

Using AI in automation

Many tools now use AI to write subject lines, suggest send times or draft emails. These features save time, but a person should review every message before it goes into a flow. Our guide to AI marketing tools shows a safe review process.

Frequently asked questions

What is marketing automation software?

It is software that sends messages and runs tasks when a trigger happens, such as a form submission or a purchase. It helps small businesses follow up quickly and consistently without doing every step by hand.

Is there free marketing automation software?

Yes. Several tools have free plans with basic email automation, such as a welcome email. Multi-step workflows with branches usually need a paid plan.

What is the difference between email marketing and marketing automation?

Email marketing sends campaigns to a list. Marketing automation runs flows triggered by each person's actions, and it can include texts, tasks and CRM updates as well as email.

Do I need a CRM for marketing automation?

It helps. A CRM keeps each contact's history in one place, so your automations can use it. Some automation tools include a simple CRM.

Yes. SEMRS writes email content and can set up welcome, follow-up and review flows in the platform you already use. See our content marketing services and pricing.
